name: Linux & Bash
description: The shell, permissions, processes, text pipelines and the scripting discipline that keeps automation safe.

modules.name: Shell & Pipelines
modules.description: Redirection, pipes, quoting and the tools that compose into one-liners.

cards.answer: `>` truncate-redirect stdout, `>>` append stdout, `2>` redirect stderr, `&>` redirect both, and `2>&1` point stderr at wherever stdout currently goes.
cards.explanation: Order matters: `cmd > file 2>&1` sends both to the file, while `cmd 2>&1 > file` sends stderr to the original stdout and only stdout to the file. Redirections are evaluated left to right.

cards.prompt: Why does this break on a file called `my report.txt`?
cards.code:
for f in $(ls); do
  mv $f ${f}.bak
done
cards.answer: Unquoted expansion word-splits on whitespace, so the name becomes two arguments. Also, parsing `ls` is unreliable. Use `for f in *; do mv -- "$f" "$f.bak"; done`.
cards.explanation: Quote every expansion unless you specifically want splitting. Add `--` before filename arguments so a file named `-rf` is not read as options. `shellcheck` catches both automatically.

cards.prompt: What does `set -euo pipefail` do, and what is the catch?
cards.answer: `-e` exits on an unhandled error, `-u` errors on unset variables, `-o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails. The catch is that `-e` has many exceptions — conditions, `&&` chains, command substitutions — so it is a safety net, not a guarantee.
cards.explanation: Pair it with `trap 'echo failed at line $LINENO' ERR` for diagnosis, and handle expected failures explicitly with `|| true`. Without `pipefail`, `false | tee log` succeeds — a genuinely dangerous default in deployment scripts.

resources.title: GNU Bash manual — The Set Builtin

cards.prompt: From a web log, find the top 10 IPs by request count. Which tools, in what order?
cards.answer: `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10` — extract the field, sort so duplicates are adjacent, count them, sort by count descending, take ten.
cards.explanation: `uniq` only collapses *adjacent* duplicates, which is why the first sort is mandatory. This cut/sort/uniq/sort pipeline answers a surprising share of ad-hoc log questions without any tooling at all.

cards.prompt: In the shell, an exit status of ___ means success and any other value means failure.
cards.explanation: `$?` holds the last status. 1 is generic failure, 2 usually misuse, 126 not executable, 127 command not found, and 128+N means killed by signal N — so 137 is SIGKILL (often the OOM killer) and 143 is SIGTERM.

modules.name: System Administration
modules.description: Permissions, processes, services and diagnosing a sick machine.

cards.prompt: What permissions does `chmod 640 file` grant?
cards.code:
$ chmod 640 secrets.env
$ ls -l secrets.env
-rw-r----- 1 alice devs 128 Sep 10 14:02 secrets.env
cards.answer: Owner read+write (6), group read (4), others nothing (0).
cards.explanation: Each digit is a bitmask: 4 read, 2 write, 1 execute. On directories, execute means 'may traverse' and read means 'may list'. 600 for private keys, 644 for public files, 755 for executables and directories — and `chmod 777` is essentially never the right answer.

cards.prompt: A server is slow. What do you check, in what order?
cards.answer: Load and CPU (`uptime`, `top`), memory and swap (`free -h`), disk I/O wait (`iostat`, `%wa` in top), disk space and inodes (`df -h`, `df -i`), network (`ss -s`), then per-process detail (`pidstat`, `strace`) and finally the logs (`journalctl -xe`, `dmesg -T`).
cards.explanation: Brendan Gregg's USE method formalises this: for every resource check Utilisation, Saturation and Errors. High load with low CPU usually means I/O wait or lock contention; a full disk and exhausted inodes both present as bizarre unrelated failures.

resources.title: Brendan Gregg — Linux performance analysis in 60 seconds

cards.prompt: What is the difference between `kill`, `kill -9` and `kill -HUP`?
cards.answer: Plain `kill` sends SIGTERM — a polite request the process can handle. `-9` sends SIGKILL, which the kernel enforces and no process can catch or clean up after. `-HUP` traditionally means 'reload your configuration'.
cards.explanation: Reaching for `-9` first skips graceful shutdown: open files unflushed, locks unreleased, in-flight requests dropped. Try SIGTERM, wait, then escalate. If SIGTERM does nothing, the process may be stuck in uninterruptible sleep (state D) — usually blocked on I/O.

cards.prompt: What does systemd give you over running a binary in a screen session?
cards.answer: Supervision and restart policies, dependency ordering, resource limits via cgroups, log capture into the journal, start on boot, and a consistent `systemctl` interface for start/stop/status/reload.
cards.explanation: Key commands: `systemctl status|start|enable|daemon-reload`, `journalctl -u <unit> -f`. The unit file's `Restart=`, `RestartSec=` and `OOMPolicy=` decide what happens when your service dies — set them deliberately rather than accepting defaults.

cards.prompt: Why is this dangerous with unusual filenames, and what is the safe form?
cards.answer: Filenames containing spaces or newlines are split into multiple arguments, so the wrong files get deleted. Use `find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 rm --` or `find . -name '*.log' -delete`.
cards.explanation: NUL is the only byte that cannot appear in a filename, which is why `-print0`/`-0` is the safe pairing. Always dry-run destructive finds with `-print` or `echo` first — `find` plus `rm` is one of the classic ways to destroy a machine.

modules.name: Filesystem, Users & Permissions
modules.description: The directory hierarchy, links, special permission bits, users and sudo, environment and PATH, and disk usage.

cards.prompt: What lives in `/etc`, `/var`, `/usr`, `/home`, `/tmp`, `/proc` and `/dev`?
cards.answer: `/etc` system configuration; `/var` variable data — logs, caches, spools, databases; `/usr` installed programs and libraries; `/home` user directories; `/tmp` temporary files (often cleared on boot); `/proc` and `/sys` virtual files exposing kernel and process state; `/dev` device files.
cards.explanation: Knowing the layout tells you where to look: config in /etc, logs in /var/log, a process's open files in /proc/<pid>/fd. `/proc` and `/sys` are generated by the kernel on demand — reading `/proc/meminfo` asks the kernel, not a disk.

cards.prompt: Hard link vs symbolic link
cards.answer: A hard link is another directory entry pointing to the same inode — the same file under two names. A symbolic link is a small file containing a path to another file.

left.title: Hard link
points: Same filesystem only; not for directories

right.title: Symlink
points: Dangles if the target is removed

cards.explanation: Deleting a file only removes one name; its data is freed when the last hard link (and last open descriptor) goes away — which is why deleting a huge log a process still holds open does not free disk space until it is restarted or the file is truncated.

cards.prompt: What do the setuid, setgid and sticky bits do?
cards.answer: setuid on an executable runs it with the file owner's privileges (`passwd` runs as root to edit the password database). setgid on a directory makes new files inherit its group. The sticky bit on a shared directory such as `/tmp` lets users delete only their own files.
cards.explanation: setuid-root binaries are prime privilege-escalation targets, so audit them (`find / -perm -4000`) and keep the list minimal. Linux capabilities (`CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` to bind port 80) grant one specific root power instead of all of them.

cards.prompt: Why use `sudo` instead of logging in as root, and what defines a user's groups?
cards.answer: sudo grants privileges per command, to named users, with every use logged and the policy in `/etc/sudoers` (edited with `visudo`). Logging in as root leaves no per-person audit trail and makes every mistake privileged. Users and groups are defined in `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group` (or a directory service).
cards.explanation: Group membership changes take effect only at the next login (or with `newgrp`), a common source of "I added myself to the docker group and it still fails". Adding a user to `docker` effectively grants root, since the Docker daemon runs as root.

cards.prompt: After running this, `ls` and every other command stop working in the shell. Why?
cards.answer: `PATH=~/bin` replaced the whole search path instead of adding to it, so the shell can no longer find `/usr/bin/ls`. Prepend or append instead: `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`.
cards.explanation: `PATH` is a colon-separated list searched in order for commands; `which -a cmd` or `type cmd` shows which one wins. Environment variables are inherited by child processes only when exported, and changes in a script do not affect the parent shell unless the script is `source`d.

resources.title: GNU Bash manual — Bourne shell variables

cards.prompt: `df -h` says the disk is 100% full, but `du -sh /*` adds up to far less. Where is the space?
cards.answer: Most likely in deleted files still held open by a running process — their space is not freed until the descriptor closes. `lsof +L1` (or `lsof | grep deleted`) lists them; restart or signal the process, or truncate via `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>`. Other causes: data hidden under a mount point, or reserved root blocks.
cards.explanation: Also check inodes with `df -i` — millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes while bytes remain free. `ncdu` gives an interactive view of what uses space.

modules.name: Shell Power Tools
modules.description: Expansion order and globbing, here-docs and process substitution, job control, scheduling, archives and the text tools.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
a b c
{a,b,c}
hello world
$name
4
cards.explanation: Brace expansion, then variable and command substitution, arithmetic expansion, word splitting and globbing happen in a fixed order, and quoting switches them off selectively: double quotes allow `$` expansion but suppress splitting and globbing; single quotes suppress everything. Quoted braces are not expanded.

cards.prompt: What are here-documents and process substitution?
cards.answer: A here-document feeds inline text as stdin: `cat <<EOF ... EOF` (quote the delimiter, `<<'EOF'`, to stop variable expansion inside). Process substitution `<(cmd)` presents a command's output as a file path, so tools expecting files can read streams: `diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)`.
cards.explanation: `<<-EOF` strips leading tabs so the here-doc can be indented. Process substitution is a Bash/Zsh feature, not POSIX `sh` — scripts using it need a `#!/usr/bin/env bash` shebang.

cards.prompt: How do `&`, `jobs`, `fg`, `bg`, Ctrl-Z and `wait` work?
cards.answer: `cmd &` starts a job in the background; Ctrl-Z suspends the foreground job; `bg` resumes it in the background and `fg` brings it back; `jobs` lists them; `wait` blocks until background jobs finish (and returns their status).
cards.explanation: Background jobs still die when the terminal closes unless protected by `nohup`, `disown`, or a multiplexer. In scripts, `cmd1 & cmd2 & wait` runs work in parallel — check each exit status with `wait $pid`, since a bare `wait` hides failures.

resources.title: GNU Bash manual — Job control basics

cards.prompt: cron vs systemd timers
cards.answer: cron runs commands on a five-field schedule (`minute hour day month weekday`) from crontabs; systemd timers trigger service units on calendar or monotonic schedules, with logging, dependencies and resource limits from systemd.

left.title: cron
points: Minimal environment; output emailed or lost
No catch-up for missed runs (anacron aside)

right.title: systemd timer
points: Logs in the journal per run

cards.explanation: cron jobs run with a minimal environment — a different PATH and no shell profile — the most common reason a script works interactively and fails from cron. Use absolute paths, redirect output somewhere, and guard against overlapping runs with `flock`.

cards.prompt: What is each of `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `cut`, `tr` and `xargs` best at?
cards.answer: `grep` filters lines by pattern; `sed` edits streams (substitute, delete lines); `awk` processes columns and does arithmetic per line; `cut` extracts fields by delimiter; `tr` translates or deletes characters; `xargs` turns input lines into command arguments.
cards.explanation: A few idioms go a long way: `grep -rn pattern dir`, `sed -i 's/old/new/g' file` (GNU; BSD sed needs `-i ''`), `awk '{sum += $3} END {print sum}'`. Modern replacements such as ripgrep and jq are faster or structure-aware, but the classics are on every server.

cards.prompt: To create a gzip-compressed archive of a directory, run `tar -___ backup.tar.gz dir/` (create, gzip, file).
cards.answer: czf
cards.explanation: `c` create, `x` extract, `t` list, `z` gzip, `J` xz, `--zstd` zstd, `f` names the archive file, `v` verbose. `tar -xzf file.tar.gz -C /dest` extracts elsewhere. zstd gives the best speed-to-ratio trade-off today; xz the smallest files at a high CPU cost.

cards.prompt: A process misbehaves in production and you cannot attach a debugger. What can `/proc/<pid>` tell you?
cards.answer: `cmdline` (exact arguments), `environ` (its environment), `fd/` (every open file and socket), `status` (state, memory, threads), `limits` (ulimits in force), `cwd` and `exe`, `stack` for the kernel stack, and `io` for read/write counters.
cards.explanation: This answers "which config did it load?", "which files and connections are open?" and "is it hitting the open-file limit?" without restarting anything. `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l` against the limit in `/proc/<pid>/limits` diagnoses descriptor leaks.
